label: Freshwater
blurb: Wetlands, groundwater-dependent ecosystems, rivers and streams, floodplains and freshwater species richness (report Table 13).

charts.title: Freshwater features
charts.subtitle: Share of each feature's extent in this area by conservation status (report Table 13)

charts.title: Rivers and streams by order
charts.subtitle: Share of stream length by conservation status (report Table 13)

method: Wetlands are the National Wetlands Inventory's freshwater emergent, freshwater forested/shrub, and estuarine and marine wetland types in California; groundwater-dependent ecosystems are the GDE vegetation and wetland layers (Klausmeyer et al. 2018). Each wetland's mapped acreage is spread evenly over the resolution-10 cells it touches, which reproduces the report's wetland shares to within 0.1 percentage point. Groundwater-dependent ecosystems are counted on whole resolution-10 cells (about 4 acres); this catalog's layer totals 2.4 million acres against the report's 4.3 million, so their extents differ while their shares in 30x30 agree to within one point. The 100-year floodplain row uses FEMA's flood hazard map (Special Flood Hazard Areas); the report used First Street Foundation flood zones, which this catalog does not carry, so the two are different features. Freshwater species richness marks HUC12 watersheds in California's top 20% (Howard et al. 2015); against the report, this row has 1 point less in 30x30 and 5 points less on GAP 3–4 land, which a different richness cutoff does not explain. Streams use the NHDPlus High Resolution network, with stream order from that network, restricted to California's land grid and measured by length: each flowline's length is spread over the cells it crosses. That network carries roughly three times the channel length of the medium-resolution network behind the report, so shares compare and lengths do not. Wetlands and groundwater-dependent ecosystems are Key Features in the report; the freshwater-richness row is a value-based feature with no need class.
